messages.subject: Problems reading my edf and tdf with data2oSCR()
messages.subject_clean: Problems reading my edf and tdf with data2oSCR()
messages.body_plain:
I have edf and tdf from scrbook that work fine, but won't read into oSCR helper function. Getting some traps in edf not showing up in tdf. They are there, so something else not working. I have fewer encounters than traps, so wondering if that is throwing the error? I tried converting session.id <http://session.id> to factors, still no joy.  Any advice would be appreciated.

Brian

messages.subject_clean: [oscr] Problems reading my edf and tdf with data2oSCR()
messages.body_plain:
hi Brian,
 if you have a trap identity in the EDF data  but it doesn't show up in your TDF then this throws an error , so just make sure your TDF contains all possible traps...  This is a common error in data formatting often due to slight differences in the trap names between separate excel files or similar.
regards
andy

messages.subject: RE: [oscr] Problems reading my edf and tdf with data2oSCR()
messages.subject_clean: [oscr] Problems reading my edf and tdf with data2oSCR()
messages.body_plain:
Hi Brian,

The following is not tested, but should be about what you need to identify the culprit.

If this is single session data, then you can use the following to

#change object (edf, tdf) and column names (trap) to match your data

edf$trap[!which(edf$trap %in% tdf$trap)]

If it’s multi-session, throw it in a loop:

#change object and column names to match your data

#also, there is a tdf per session, so let’s assume you wrapped them in a list:

tdf.ls <http://tdf.ls> <- list(tdf1, tdf2,etc, )

for(i in 1:length(unique(edf$session))){

  tmp.sesh <- unique(edf$session)[i]

  tmp.edf <- subset(edf, session == tmp.sesh)

  tmp.edf$trap[!which(tmp.edf$trap %in% tdf.ls <http://tdf.ls>[[i]]$trap)]

}

messages.subject: RE: [oscr] Pooling sessions
messages.body_plain:
Hi Clayton,

We did some of ‘structured pooling’ in our mink paper <https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-018-26847-x> and our cheetah paper <https://esj-journals.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1002/1438-390X.12045>. If I understand correctly, I think the following fabricated example is one approach.

Let’s say we have 6 session, 3 in protected areas, 3 outside. The inference objective is to test whether density, sigma, or detection vary by protection status. So, without any covariates, we can easily estimate constant parameters (no variation, D~1) or, using the built in model ‘~Session’, we can estimate session-specific parameters. NB: this works for p0, Sig, and D. But, we can also so a lot more through creative covariate generation. Here is a way to add covariates to pool the protected and not protected sessions (‘Prot’ ‘uProt’, respectively).

Density:

#6 sessions: 1-3 are Prot, 4-6 are uProt

# ssDF is the ssDF object

prot <- rep(c(‘Prot’,’uProt’),each=3)

for(i in 1:6){

  ssDF[[i]]$prot <- factor(prot[i],levels= c(‘Prot’,’uProt’))

}

Now you can specify ~prot in the density model and estimate an intercept (Prot) and the coefficient (contract) for not protected. Likewise, you could add continuous variable to estimate effects (latitude for example).

Sigma:

#6 sessions: 1-3 are Prot, 4-6 are uProt

# scrFrame is the scrFrame object

# sigCovs is a dataframe with nSession rows, and nCovaraite columns.

# i.e., sigCovs is like a session covariate data frame

scrFrame$sigCovs$prot <- factor(rep(c(‘Prot’,’uProt’),each=3)) #adding the new covariate here

Now you can specify ~prot in the sigma model and estimate an intercept (Prot) and the coefficient (contract) for not protected. Likewise, you could add continuous variable to estimate effects (latitude for example).

Baseline encounter (p0/g0):

In this case, following the same idea, you can add covariates to the tdf (add a column called prot, giving all traps is a session the same value). Now you can specify ~prot in the detection model and estimate an intercept (Prot) and the coefficient (contract) for not protected. Likewise, you could add continuous variable to estimate effects (latitude for example).

Using this approach gives a huge amount of flexibility in terms of ‘structured pooling’ beyond the simple ‘all or session’ approach that the majority of applications default to.

Hope this helps, but if I’m way off the mark, let me know and I can have another go.

Chris
